newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says aid to east Germany to continue.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says aid to east Germany to continue.

text.p: Six years after unification, eastern Germany's recovery is slowing, and more state aid will be needed to help the region overcome the legacy of 40 years of communist central planning, a government report said Wednesday.

Germany is in the midst of a clash with the European Commission over awarding state aid to two Volkswagen car plants in the eastern state of Saxony, but the report said there was no alternative to further handouts.
"The federal government will resolutely continue its growth- and jobs-oriented strategy, and above all make available the necessary funds," the report said.
Eastern Germany is still beset by high unemployment, unit labour costs over 30 percent higher than in the west and a weak industrial base and infrastructure, the report said.
The 70-page document was drawn up by the economics ministry and approved at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday.
Huge financial transfers kept one million people off the dole last year, but subsidies will eventually be wound down to restore a level playing field to the European single market.
"The debate over the VW Saxony investment project must not become a misplaced and dangerous fundamental struggle between rebuilding the east and unifying Europe," the report said.
Net financial transfers to eastern Germany peaked at 172 billion marks in 1993, and will fall to 144 billion marks this year and 138 billion marks in 1997.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said after the cabinet meeting that the government would have to make further funds available to help east Germany rebuild after next year -- but neither he nor the report gave any details.
The report said that after a runaway post-unification construction boom, the base of the east German economy should shift more to the industrial sector.
That would mean more moderate growth -- which is forecast this year at three percent after 5.3 percent last year and 9.9 percent in 1994.

The report conceded that controversial job creation measures "create no permanent and competitive jobs" and that financial support would be up for discussion in budget talks this autumn. Labour creation spending is down to 27 billion marks this year from 42 billion in 1993.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said further spending cuts have to be made on top of a 70 billion mark austerity package intended to qualify Germany for European economic and monetary union next year. The 1997 budget will have its final reading in November.

The report also said eastern Germany was living far beyond its means. The region's gross domestic product makes up only two-thirds of total consumption -- below poorer European Union member states like Portugal and Greece.
It also said that there could be no quick fix for a jump in unit labour costs resulting from a rise in wages towards western levels while labour productivity growth has lagged.
"The greatest obstacle to rapid economic development in eastern Germany remains excessively high unit labour costs," the report said.
